title: God tends a changing world like a farmer through the seasons
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα λέγει ὅτι οὔτε τὰ ὁρώμενα ἀνθρώπῳ δέδοται, ἀλλ᾿ ἕκαστα τοῦ ὅλου σωτηρίας εἵνεκα γίνεταί τε καὶ ἀπόλλυται καθ᾿ ἣν προεῖπον ἀμοιβὴν ἐξ ἀλλήλων εἰς ἄλληλα· περισσὸν δὲ τὸ προσδιατρίβειν τῇ τούτων ἀνατροπῇ, κατὰ δύναμιν ἡμῖν προεκτεθείσῃ. εἴρηται δὲ καὶ εἰς τοῦτο· οὔτε δὲ τὰ ἀγαθὰ οὔτε τὰ κακὰ ἐν τοῖς θνητοῖς ἐλάττω ἢ πλείω γένοιτ᾿ ἄν. λέλεκται καὶ εἰς τό· οὔτε τῷ θεῷ καινοτέρας δεῖ διορθώσεως. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ὡς ἄνθρωπος τεκτηνάμενός τι ἐνδεῶς καὶ ἀτεχνότερον δημιουργήσας ὁ θεὸς προσάγει διόρθωσιν τῷ κόσμῳ, καθαίρων αὐτὸν κατακλυσμῷ ἢ ἐκπυρώσει, ἀλλὰ τὴν χύσιν τῆς κακίας κωλύων ἐπὶ πλεῖον νέμεσθαι, ἐγὼ δ᾿ οἶμαι ὅτι καὶ πάντῃ τεταγμένως αὐτὴν ἀφανίζων συμφερόντως τῷ παντί. εἰ δὲ μετὰ τὸν ἀφανισμὸν τῆς κακίας λόγον ἔχει τὸ πάλιν αὐτὴν ὑφίστασθαι η μὴ, ἐν προηγουμένῳ λόγῳ τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐξετασθήσεται. θέλει οὖν διὰ καινοτέρας διορθώσεως ἀεὶ ὁ θεὸς τὰ σφάλματα ἀναλαμβάνειν. εἰ γὰρ καὶ τέτακται αὐτῷ πάντα κάλλιστα καὶ ἀσφαλέστατα κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργίαν, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν ἧττον ἰατρικῆς τινος αὐτῷ ἐδέησε τοῖς τὴν κακίαν νοσοῦσι καὶ παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ, ὑπ᾿ αὐτῆς ὡσπερεὶ μολυνομένῳ, καὶ οὐδέν γε ἠμέληται τῷ θεῷ ἢ ἀμεληθήσεται, ποιοῦντι καθ᾿ ἕκαστον καιρὸν ὅπερ ἔπρεπεν αὐτὸν ποιεῖν ἐν τρεπτῷ καὶ μεταβλητῷ κόσμῳ. καὶ ὥσπερ γεωργὸς κατὰ τὰς διαφόρους τῶν τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ὡρῶν διάφορα ἔργα γεωργικὰ ποιεῖ ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ τὰ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς φυόμενα, οὕτως ὁ θεὸς οἱονεὶ ἐνιαυτούς τινας, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω. οἰκονομεῖ ὅλους τοὺς αἰῶνας. καθ᾿ ἕκαστον αὐτῶν ποιῶν ὅσα ἀπαιτεῖ αὐτὸ τὸ περὶ τὰ ὅλα εὔλογον, ὑπὸ μόνου θεοῦ ὡς ἀληθείας ἔχει τρανότατα καταλαμβανόμενον καὶ ἐπιτελούμενον.
pass_a_gloss: After these he says that [Celsus:] neither have the things seen (τὰ ὁρώμενα) been given (δίδωμι) to man (ἄνθρωπος), but each thing for the sake of the preservation (σωτηρία) of the whole (τὸ ὅλον) comes to be and perishes (ἀπόλλυμαι) according to the exchange (ἀμοιβή) I spoke of before, from one another into one another. Superfluous (περισσός) to spend further time (προσδιατρίβω) on the overturning (ἀνατροπή) of these, set out before by us according to ability. It has been said also against this: [Celsus:] neither the good things nor the evil things among mortals could become fewer or more. It has been said also against: [Celsus:] nor does God need (δεῖ) a newer correction (καινοτέρα διόρθωσις). But not as a man having built (τεκταίνομαι) something deficiently (ἐνδεῶς) and having crafted (δημιουργέω) more unskilfully (ἀτεχνότερον) does God bring correction to the world, cleansing (καθαίρω) it by flood (κατακλυσμός) or conflagration (ἐκπύρωσις), but preventing (κωλύω) the outpouring (χύσις) of evil (κακία) from spreading (νέμομαι) further; and I think also wholly (πάντῃ) in an orderly way (τεταγμένως) making it vanish (ἀφανίζω) beneficially (συμφερόντως) to the all. Whether after the vanishing (ἀφανισμός) of evil there is reason (λόγον ἔχει) for it to subsist (ὑφίσταμαι) again or not, in a principal treatment (προηγούμενος λόγος) such things will be examined. God therefore wills (θέλω) through newer correction always to take up again (ἀναλαμβάνω) the errors (σφάλματα). For even if all things were ordered by him most beautifully and most securely (ἀσφαλέστατα) in the crafting (δημιουργία) of the universe (τὰ ὅλα), nonetheless he needed some medical art (ἰατρική) for those sick (νοσέω) with evil and the whole world, as it were stained (μολύνω) by it; and nothing has been neglected (ἀμελέω) by God or will be, doing at each time (καιρός) what was fitting (πρέπω) for him to do in a changeable (τρεπτός) and alterable (μεταβλητός) world. And as a farmer (γεωργός) according to the different seasons (ὧραι) of the year (ἐνιαυτός) does different farm works on the earth and what grows on it, so God, as it were certain years, so to name it, administers (οἰκονομέω) whole ages (αἰῶνες), doing in each of them as much as the reasonable order (τὸ εὔλογον) concerning the whole itself demands (ἀπαιτέω), which by God alone, as truth holds, is most clearly (τρανότατα) grasped (καταλαμβάνω) and accomplished (ἐπιτελέω).
pass_b_english: After this he says: “Nor have the things that are seen been given to man; but each thing comes into being and perishes for the sake of the preservation of the whole, according to the exchange I spoke of before, from one into another.” It is superfluous to spend more time refuting this, since we have already set out the refutation as best we could.

A reply has also been given to this: “Neither good things nor evil things among mortals could become fewer or more.” And we have spoken as well to this: “Nor does God need a new correction.” But God does not, like a man who has built something defectively and made it with too little skill, apply a correction to the world when he cleanses it by a flood or a conflagration. Rather, he is checking the outpouring of evil so that it spreads no further; and I think that he is also doing away with it altogether, in due order, to the benefit of the whole. Whether, after evil has been done away with, there is reason for it to come into being again or not, such questions will be examined in a discussion devoted to them.

So God does indeed always will to repair faults by a new correction. For even if everything was ordered by him in the most beautiful and most secure way in the making of the universe, he nonetheless needed a kind of healing art for those sick with evil and for the whole world, which evil has, as it were, defiled. And nothing has been neglected by God, or will be neglected, since at each time he does what it was fitting for him to do in a world that is changeable and subject to alteration.

And just as a farmer does different kinds of farm work on the land and on what grows from it according to the different seasons of the year, so God orders whole ages as if they were, so to speak, years, doing in each of them whatever the reasonable order of the universe itself requires, which God alone grasps most clearly, as it truly is, and carries out.

choices.choice: 'preventing the flood of evil from spreading further' made 'checking the outpouring of evil so that it spreads no further' (χύσις; avoids two senses of 'flood' in one sentence)
'God, then, does will always to set faults right' (stiff order) made 'So God does indeed always will to repair faults'
'governs' made 'orders' (οἰκονομεῖ); 'the reason that governs the universe' made 'the reasonable order of the universe itself' (αὐτὸ τὸ περὶ τὰ ὅλα εὔλογον, nearer the Greek)
'as the truth is' made 'as it truly is', attached to 'grasps'
Celsus quotations and 'I spoke of before' (Celsus's first person) checked as correctly framed

Three short quotations of Celsus (quoted in double marks); the replies Origen refers to (‘has been said’, ‘we have spoken’) are earlier in this book, around 4.62–4.65. ‘καθ᾽ ἣν προεῖπον ἀμοιβήν’: the first person is Celsus’s (‘I spoke of before’), so it stays inside his quotation. ‘οὔτε τῷ θεῷ καινοτέρας δεῖ διορθώσεως’: the comparative καινοτέρας rendered ‘new’ (a fresh correction). Origen’s answer then turns the phrase: God ‘does will’ (θέλει) to correct faults ‘by a new correction’. The flood and conflagration are those of the cosmic theory Celsus has been using (Book 4.11 onward); Origen does not point to a particular verse here, so the flood is not given a Genesis citation. ‘χύσιν τῆς κακίας … νέμεσθαι’ uses the image of something spreading like a flood or a sore; rendered ‘checking the outpouring of evil so that it spreads no further’ (χύσις = outpouring; ‘flood’ avoided so it is not confused with the literal flood just before). ‘ἐν προηγουμένῳ λόγῳ’ = ‘in a discussion devoted to them’. The final clause (‘τὸ περὶ τὰ ὅλα εὔλογον’) taken as ‘the reasonable order of the universe’; ‘ὡς ἀληθείας ἔχει’ = ‘as it truly is’, taken with ‘grasps’.
